kurz: Hedge funds and private equity market themselves on exclusivity; how much of their return reaches the investor depends on the fee structure and on the metric used to measure the return.

bloecke.md:
The return a manager generates and the return that reaches the investor are two different figures. For a broad index ETF, they are around 0.2 percentage points apart. For a hedge fund with the classic fee structure, the gap is two to five points depending on the result, and even more for a fund of funds. Assessing these asset classes therefore starts with the fee structure and only then with the strategy.

The classic fee structure is abbreviated as **2/20**. It stands for 2% of assets under management a year, charged regardless of the result, plus 20% of the profit. The 2% is therefore also due in loss-making years. The 20% is a one-sided participation, because the manager receives a share of the profit but bears no share of the loss. Economically, this is equivalent to a call option on the fund assets that is issued anew every year and for which the manager pays nothing. This asymmetry is the most important feature of the fee structure.

bloecke.md: How heavily this deduction weighs depends on the size of the result. The management fee is fixed, while the performance fee grows with the profit. Together, the two take the largest proportion of the return in weak years. At a gross return of 4%, the manager keeps 60% of the return; at 16%, only 30%. For a fund that aims to make money independently of the market and targets rather modest gross returns, most of the return therefore goes on fees.

bloecke.titel: Effect of fees by gross result (2/20, no hurdle)

bloecke.md: A gross return of 8% a year over ten years produces a total gain of 115.9%. After deducting 2/20, 4.8% net a year remains, and thus a total gain of 59.8%. The investor bears the entire risk and receives just over half of the return. The fees thus reduce the total gain by 48%. Around 40% of the initial capital is paid out in fees over the ten years; the rest of the gap is compound interest forgone on these fees. A fund of funds adds a second layer of fees.

## The Buffett bet

On 19 December 2007, Warren Buffett entered into a publicly documented bet. He predicted that over ten years a simple S&P 500 index fund would beat a group of funds of hedge funds selected by professionals. The other side, Protégé Partners, chose five funds of funds that together held stakes in more than two hundred individual hedge funds. The selection thus offered maximum diversification, top talent and the ability to reallocate at any time.

From 2008 to 2017, the index fund achieved a total gain of 125.8%, or 8.5% a year. The five funds of funds achieved 21.7%, 42.3%, 87.7%, 2.8% and 27.0%, which is between 0.3% and 6.5% a year. Only in the crash year 2008 was every one of them ahead of the index. Over the following nine years taken together, all of them were behind. Buffett sees the cause in fixed fees of around 2.5% of assets a year, charged regardless of the result, and does not consider the managers themselves to be bad.

bloecke.md:
The bet is a cleanly documented single case covering a single ten-year period. In Buffett's assessment, this period was not unusual for US equities, because forecasts made at the end of 2007 would on average have expected roughly the 8.5% a year that was actually achieved. The bet demonstrates the effect of the fee burden but leaves open whether good management is possible.

Reliable overall statistics are harder to obtain than for retail funds, because hedge funds report their figures to commercial databases voluntarily. Funds with poor results stop reporting. Newly added funds may add their previous history retrospectively (backfill). Both effects bias any index calculated from these data upwards, and neither can be cleanly removed from the outside. For sweeping statements about “the hedge fund return”, you should therefore always establish which database the figure comes from.

## Private equity and the internal rate of return

Private equity works differently. The investor signs a capital commitment, say €500,000, and does not pay it in immediately. The fund calls the money in tranches over four to five years, uses it to buy companies, holds them for five to seven years and pays back the proceeds. The total term is ten to twelve years. Exiting earlier is only possible via the secondary market, often at a discount. In the first years, fees and incidental purchase costs are set against valuations that do not yet include any increase in value. The value of the investment therefore falls at first and only rises later, a pattern known as the J-curve.

Because the payments are irregular, the return is stated as the **internal rate of return** (IRR). The IRR is a money-weighted return. It depends on the timing and size of the payments and rewards a short period of capital commitment. This opens up a structuring option that investors usually do not notice. Many funds initially finance their purchases through a bank credit line and only call the capital a year later. This reduces the profit in euros by the interest on the loan, while the reported IRR rises.

bloecke.titel: The same deal with two return figures (illustrative calculation)

bloecke.md:
Without a credit line: 200 / 100 = 2.00. Its fifth root is 1.1487, which is 14.9% a year.

With a credit line: 200 / 105 = 1.9048. Its fourth root is 1.1748, which is 17.5% a year.

The investor earns €5 less and is shown a return that is 2.6 percentage points higher. The multiple (amount paid back divided by amount paid in) is therefore the more meaningful metric, because it cannot be improved by shifting the timing.

Two further points are needed to put this in context. The first is debt. A debt-financed company acquisition is equivalent to a leveraged equity position. Part of the excess return over the stock market is thus payment for additional risk taken on and has nothing to do with skill. The same logic lies behind the observation that access to credit systematically creates differences in returns. The second point is **appraisal smoothing**. Unlisted holdings are not traded continuously; their value is determined quarterly by appraisers. As a result, the measured volatility and the measured correlation with the stock market come out low. In an optimisation model, the asset class therefore looks better than it is and receives too high a weighting. The risk still exists; the infrequent valuations simply fail to capture it.

The **public market equivalent** therefore serves as a clean benchmark. It involves investing the same cash flows at the same times in an equity index and comparing the final values. Using this method, critics such as Ludovic Phalippou find results close to the stock market for the fund vintages since the financial crisis, but with considerably higher fees and capital tied up for ten years. The opposing view has arguments that deserve to be taken seriously. A majority owner can steer a company instead of just watching, and many medium-sized companies cannot be reached via the stock exchange at all. Both points justify the existence of the asset class. But they do not establish that any given fund makes these advantages available to a private investor.

bloecke.unter: Each level charges its own fees; the return advertised is almost always that of the target fund, but the investor only receives the return after all levels have been deducted.

## Access and taxes in Germany

Under the KAGB (German Investment Code), the classic hedge fund is a general open-ended domestic special AIF (Spezial-AIF) whose investment terms provide for leverage on a substantial scale or for short selling (Section 283 KAGB). The leverage is not unlimited, because the fund management company (KVG) must set and comply with a ceiling, and BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) can restrict it further (Section 29(4) and Section 274 KAGB). Special AIFs are only open to professional and semi-professional investors. Under Section 1(19) no. 33 KAGB, you generally only qualify as a semi-professional investor with an investment of at least €200,000 and after a documented suitability assessment by the fund management company. Private equity reaches private investors through closed-ended retail AIFs, which may only be acquired from €20,000 upwards if they are not diversified (Section 262(2) KAGB). Since 10 January 2024, the ELTIF 2.0 has also been available (Regulation (EU) 2015/760 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/606). This revision abolished the former minimum investment of €10,000 and the 10% limit for retail investors. Access is therefore open, but that does not change the quality of the funds on offer.

bloecke.titel: Four fund types and their rules
zeilen: depending on structure, Section 20 or Section 15 EStG
no statutory minimum amount any more
InvStG, partial exemption only with a qualifying equity ratio
InvStG, Section 20 InvStG according to equity ratio

bloecke.md: For tax purposes, German private investors face a double disadvantage with these products. The 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) is only available to equity funds, and a fund only counts as an equity fund if it continuously invests more than 50% of its assets in equity participations (Section 2(6) InvStG). Market-neutral strategies, credit funds and most fund-of-funds structures do not meet this condition. If they continuously invest at least 25% in equity participations, they count as mixed funds with a 15% partial exemption (Section 2(7) and Section 20(2) InvStG). Otherwise, their income is subject to the full flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d EStG (Income Tax Act), that is 25% plus solidarity surcharge, together 26.375%. For an equity ETF, the effective rate is 18.46%. In the ETF, an 8% gross return becomes 6.52% after tax. A fund without partial exemption has to earn 8.86%, that is 0.86 points more, to draw level after tax. With accumulating structures, the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) under Section 18 InvStG comes on top. It triggers tax before any money has flowed to the investor. For a fund you cannot exit for ten years, this creates a liquidity problem of its own.

The manager's 20% profit share is called carried interest. For asset-managing venture capital and private equity partnerships, Section 18(1) no. 4 EStG treats it as income from self-employment (Einkünfte aus selbständiger Arbeit). Under Section 3 no. 40a EStG, 40% of it remains tax-free. The manager pays tax on the remaining 60% at their personal tax rate. At the top tax rate of 45%, including solidarity surcharge, this comes to around 28.5% of the carried interest, slightly more than the 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax that the investor pays on capital income. The profit share is favoured compared with a salary, on which around 47.5% is due at the top tax rate. Whether this unequal treatment is justified has been politically disputed for years. It has no effect on the investor's return calculation, but it is central to understanding the incentives.

- The return advertised is often that of the target fund. Investors should ask for the net return after feeder, fund-of-funds and distribution fees, which can be found in the PRIIPs key information document.
- Besides the IRR, the multiple (TVPI) belongs in the figures provided; otherwise the information is incomplete. Investors should also ask explicitly whether the fund uses credit lines.
- The only fair benchmark is a public market equivalent against a world equity index. The statement “We were in the top quartile” only says something about how the peer group was chosen.
- The money is tied up for ten to twelve years, and exiting is only possible via the secondary market. This commitment has to fit into the rest of your financial planning without that planning having to be rearranged for it.

In both asset classes there are managers who create value over the long term. They are rare, their funds are usually closed to new investors, and access to them is not allocated via distribution platforms. Private investors are offered the other funds, with the same fee structure but without the same quality. An asset class whose average does not beat the stock market after costs only makes sense if you have good reason to assume that you have above-average access. This assumption is justified for very few investors.

mitnehmen: With a 2/20 fee structure, the manager keeps more than half of the return in low-return years, and the management fee is also charged in loss-making years.
At an 8% gross return, the fees reduce the total gain over ten years by around 48%, through payments of around 40% of the initial capital and the compound interest forgone on them.

The Buffett bet ended with a total gain of 125.8% for the index fund against 2.8% to 87.7% for the funds of funds; as a documented single case, it shows the effect of fees but does not prove that all managers are incompetent.
The IRR can be improved with credit lines without the investor earning a single euro more, whereas the multiple and the public market equivalent cannot.
Unlisted holdings are valued less often, but that does not make their economic fluctuations any smaller.
Without the partial exemption under Section 20 InvStG, an alternative fund needs around 0.9 percentage points more gross return than an equity ETF returning 8% to draw level after tax.

begriffe.text: Highest unit value a fund has ever reached. After a loss, a performance fee with a high watermark is only charged again once this level has been exceeded. Without this rule, the investor pays twice for the same gain.

Profit share of the fund management, usually 20% of the return above a hurdle. In Germany, for asset-managing venture capital companies it is taxed under Section 18(1) no. 4 EStG, with 40% remaining tax-free under Section 3 no. 40a EStG.

Request by a closed-ended fund for the investor to pay in part of the subscribed commitment. The timing of the call determines how long the capital is tied up and thus the reported internal rate of return.

Comparison method in which the payments into and out of a closed-ended fund are invested in an equity index on the same dates and the final values are compared. It is the only method that fairly compares irregular cash flows with the stock market.

Consequence of valuation by appraisers instead of by market prices. The measured volatility and the measured correlation with the stock market come out too low as a result, although the economic risk is unchanged.
